chapter_text:
CHAPTER 2 - THE KINGDOMS MONERA, PROTOCTISTA AND FUNGI

Introduction

When R. H. Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom system of classification in 1969, he grouped living organisms on the basis of cell structure (prokaryotic or eukaryotic), body organisation (unicellular or multicellular), mode of nutrition (autotrophic or heterotrophic) and phylogenetic relationships. Three of these kingdoms - Monera, Protoctista (Protista) and Fungi - contain the simplest and most ancient forms of life. This chapter describes each of them in turn, together with a brief note on viruses, which are acellular and therefore stand outside the five kingdoms. Although microscopic and often overlooked, these organisms drive the cycling of nutrients, cause and cure disease, ferment our food, and form partnerships with plants that keep ecosystems alive.

2.1 KINGDOM MONERA

Kingdom Monera includes all the PROKARYOTES - organisms whose cells have NO true membrane-bound nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, chloroplasts or endoplasmic reticulum. Their single circular DNA molecule lies naked in the cytoplasm in a region called the NUCLEOID. Monerans are the most abundant micro-organisms on Earth, found in every habitat - soil, water, air, hot springs, deep oceans, snow and even inside other organisms. The kingdom includes bacteria, cyanobacteria (blue-green algae), archaebacteria and mycoplasmas.

BACTERIA - SHAPE AND SIZE

Bacteria are the most numerous of all organisms. A single gram of soil may contain millions of them. They are extremely small, usually 1 to 10 micrometres long. On the basis of shape bacteria are grouped into four types: (1) COCCUS - spherical or oval cells (for example Streptococcus), which may occur singly, in pairs (diplococci), in chains (streptococci) or in grape-like clusters (staphylococci); (2) BACILLUS - rod-shaped cells (for example Bacillus, Lactobacillus); (3) SPIRILLUM - rigid spiral or coiled cells (for example Spirillum); and (4) VIBRIO - comma-shaped or curved cells (for example Vibrio cholerae, which causes cholera).

BACTERIAL CELL STRUCTURE

A bacterial cell is bounded on the outside by a rigid CELL WALL made of PEPTIDOGLYCAN (murein), a network of sugars and amino acids that gives the cell its shape and protects it from bursting. Many bacteria have an extra gelatinous CAPSULE or slime layer outside the wall that helps them stick to surfaces and resist the host's defences. Inside the wall lies the PLASMA MEMBRANE, which controls what enters and leaves the cell and carries out respiration (there being no mitochondria). The cytoplasm contains RIBOSOMES (of the 70S type) for protein synthesis, food reserves, and the nucleoid with the main circular chromosome. Many bacteria also carry small extra circular DNA molecules called PLASMIDS, which often bear genes for antibiotic resistance. Some bacteria bear one or more whip-like FLAGELLA for movement, and fine hair-like PILI (fimbriae) that help them attach to surfaces or to another cell during conjugation. Under harsh conditions certain bacteria (such as Bacillus and Clostridium) form a thick-walled resting ENDOSPORE that survives heat, drought and chemicals for years and germinates when conditions improve.

GRAM-POSITIVE AND GRAM-NEGATIVE BACTERIA

In 1884 Christian Gram devised a staining method that divides bacteria into two great groups. GRAM-POSITIVE bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall and retain the violet stain, appearing purple. GRAM-NEGATIVE bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer covered by an outer membrane of lipopolysaccharide; they lose the violet stain and take up the red counterstain, appearing pink. The Gram reaction reflects a real difference in wall architecture and strongly influences which antibiotics will work against a given bacterium.

NUTRITION IN BACTERIA

Bacteria show enormous nutritional variety. AUTOTROPHIC bacteria make their own food: PHOTOAUTOTROPHS (such as the purple and green sulphur bacteria) use light energy, while CHEMOAUTOTROPHS (such as the nitrifying bacteria Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter) obtain energy by oxidising inorganic substances like ammonia, nitrite or sulphur. The majority of bacteria are HETEROTROPHIC and depend on ready-made organic food. Of these, SAPROPHYTIC bacteria feed on dead organic matter and cause decay; PARASITIC bacteria live in or on a host and often cause disease; and SYMBIOTIC bacteria live in mutually beneficial partnerships, such as Rhizobium in the root nodules of legumes and Escherichia coli in the human intestine.

REPRODUCTION IN BACTERIA

Bacteria reproduce mainly ASEXUALLY by BINARY FISSION: the circular DNA is copied and the cell divides into two identical daughter cells. Under ideal conditions a bacterium may divide every 20 minutes, so populations grow explosively. Some bacteria form endospores to survive bad conditions. True sexual reproduction is absent, but bacteria can exchange genes by three processes that create genetic variation. In CONJUGATION, two cells join through a tube (formed with the help of a sex pilus) and a copy of DNA (often a plasmid) passes from a donor to a recipient. In TRANSFORMATION, a cell takes up free DNA from the surroundings. In TRANSDUCTION, bacterial DNA is carried from one cell to another by a bacteriophage (virus). These processes spread useful genes, including antibiotic resistance, through bacterial populations.

ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE OF BACTERIA

Bacteria are both harmful and immensely useful. USEFUL ROLES include: decomposition of dead matter and recycling of nutrients; NITROGEN FIXATION by Rhizobium and free-living Azotobacter, which enriches the soil; production of curd and cheese by Lactobacillus (lactic acid bacteria); manufacture of vinegar, antibiotics (such as streptomycin from Streptomyces), vitamins and enzymes; retting of fibres; and modern uses in genetic engineering, where bacteria are used to make insulin and other products. HARMFUL ROLES include spoilage of food and human diseases such as tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), cholera (Vibrio cholerae), typhoid (Salmonella typhi), tetanus (Clostridium tetani) and pneumonia; plant diseases such as citrus canker; and animal diseases such as anthrax.

2.2 ARCHAEBACTERIA, CYANOBACTERIA AND MYCOPLASMA

ARCHAEBACTERIA versus EUBACTERIA. Kingdom Monera is often split into two lines. ARCHAEBACTERIA ('ancient bacteria') are the oldest living prokaryotes and live in extreme, hostile habitats. They differ from other bacteria in the chemistry of their cell wall (they LACK peptidoglycan) and cell membrane, which lets them survive extreme conditions. They include METHANOGENS, which produce methane gas in marshes and in the guts of cattle; HALOPHILES, which thrive in very salty water; and THERMOACIDOPHILES, which live in hot, acidic springs. All the remaining, 'true' bacteria - with peptidoglycan walls - are called EUBACTERIA.

CYANOBACTERIA (BLUE-GREEN ALGAE). Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes that contain chlorophyll a and the blue pigment phycocyanin, giving many of them a blue-green colour. They may be single-celled, colonial or filamentous (such as Nostoc, Anabaena, Oscillatoria and Spirulina), and are often surrounded by a gelatinous sheath. They carry out oxygen-releasing photosynthesis and are believed to have first oxygenated the Earth's early atmosphere. Many filamentous forms possess special thick-walled cells called HETEROCYSTS that FIX atmospheric nitrogen into a usable form; this makes cyanobacteria natural fertilisers in paddy fields. In nutrient-rich water they multiply rapidly to form 'algal blooms' or water blooms that can pollute the water. Spirulina is grown as a protein-rich food supplement.

MYCOPLASMA. Mycoplasmas are the SMALLEST known free-living cells and the simplest of all organisms. They are unique among prokaryotes in having NO CELL WALL, so their shape is variable (pleomorphic) and they are unaffected by antibiotics such as penicillin that act on the wall. Many mycoplasmas can survive without oxygen. Some are harmless, but others cause diseases in plants and animals, including pleuropneumonia in cattle.

2.3 KINGDOM PROTOCTISTA (PROTISTA)

Kingdom Protoctista (also called Protista) contains simple EUKARYOTES - organisms whose cells have a true, membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Most are UNICELLULAR, though some are colonial or simple multicellular forms. They live mainly in water or in moist places and form a link between the prokaryotic Monera and the more advanced kingdoms of plants, fungi and animals. The kingdom is a mixed assemblage that includes the animal-like protozoa, the plant-like photosynthetic protists (algal protists) and the fungus-like slime moulds.

PROTOZOA (ANIMAL-LIKE PROTISTS). Protozoa are heterotrophic, mostly free-living single-celled organisms grouped by their means of locomotion. AMOEBA (a sarcodine) has no fixed shape and moves and feeds using PSEUDOPODIA - temporary finger-like extensions of its cytoplasm - by which it engulfs food particles in a process called phagocytosis. It reproduces by binary fission. PARAMECIUM (a ciliate) is slipper-shaped and covered with thousands of tiny beating hairs called CILIA that drive it through water and sweep food into an oral groove; it is unusual in having TWO nuclei (a large macronucleus and a small micronucleus) and it can exchange genetic material by conjugation. PLASMODIUM is a sporozoan parasite that has no organs of locomotion; it is carried by the female Anopheles mosquito and causes MALARIA in humans. Other flagellated protozoa such as Trypanosoma cause sleeping sickness. Protozoa are important in food chains and some cause serious diseases.

2.4 PHOTOSYNTHETIC PROTISTS AND SLIME MOULDS

PHOTOSYNTHETIC (PLANT-LIKE) PROTISTS carry chlorophyll and make their own food, forming a large part of the floating PHYTOPLANKTON that is the base of aquatic food chains and a major source of the world's oxygen. CHLAMYDOMONAS is a single-celled green alga with two flagella, a cup-shaped chloroplast and a light-sensitive eyespot. DIATOMS are golden-brown algae enclosed in beautiful, two-piece cell walls made of silica that fit together like a soap-box; their indestructible walls pile up on sea floors as 'diatomaceous earth', used as a polishing agent and filter. DINOFLAGELLATES are mostly marine, spinning through the water with two flagellae; some are luminescent, and certain species multiply into 'red tides' that release toxins and kill fish. EUGLENOIDS such as Euglena are remarkable intermediates: they have a green chloroplast and photosynthesise in the light, but in the dark they lose the pigment and feed like animals on organic matter. Euglena has a flexible protein layer called a pellicle instead of a rigid wall, a flagellum and an eyespot.

SLIME MOULDS (FUNGUS-LIKE PROTISTS) are saprophytic organisms of damp, shady places. Under suitable conditions the body of an acellular slime mould is a naked, creeping mass of multinucleate protoplasm called a PLASMODIUM (not to be confused with the malarial parasite) that flows over rotting leaves and logs engulfing organic particles. When the surroundings dry out, the plasmodium stops and forms many stalked FRUITING BODIES that produce resistant SPORES with true walls; the spores disperse and germinate when conditions become favourable again. Slime moulds thus show features of both protozoa and fungi.

2.5 KINGDOM FUNGI

Kingdom Fungi contains eukaryotic, non-green (non-photosynthetic) organisms that live mainly on land. Because they lack chlorophyll they cannot make their own food and are all HETEROTROPHS. Fungi range from the microscopic single-celled yeasts to moulds, mushrooms, bracket fungi and puffballs.

STRUCTURE. Except for the unicellular yeasts, the body of a fungus is made of fine, thread-like filaments called HYPHAE. A tangled network or mass of hyphae is a MYCELIUM, which spreads through the food (soil, wood, bread, a host's tissues) and absorbs nutrients over a large surface. Hyphae may be divided into cells by cross-walls called SEPTA (septate hyphae) or be continuous tubes of multinucleate cytoplasm without cross-walls (coenocytic or aseptate hyphae). The cell wall of fungi is made not of cellulose but of CHITIN, the same tough material found in the outer skeleton of insects. Reserve food is stored as GLYCOGEN and oil, never as starch.

NUTRITION. All fungi are heterotrophic and absorb food after digesting it OUTSIDE the body (extracellular digestion): they secrete enzymes onto the food, which is broken down and then absorbed. There are three modes. SAPROPHYTIC fungi (such as Rhizopus and Mucor) feed on dead organic matter and are important decomposers. PARASITIC fungi live on or in a living host and cause disease in plants (rusts, smuts) and animals (ringworm). SYMBIOTIC fungi live in mutually beneficial partnerships, as in LICHENS and MYCORRHIZAE.

REPRODUCTION. Fungi reproduce by fragmentation, by asexual spores and by sexual spores. VEGETATIVE reproduction occurs by fragmentation of the mycelium, by budding (in yeast) or by fission. ASEXUAL reproduction is chiefly by SPORES - non-motile spores called conidia or aplanospores, or spores formed inside a sporangium (sporangiospores); a few water fungi form motile zoospores. SEXUAL reproduction involves the fusion of two compatible nuclei and typically passes through three stages - PLASMOGAMY (fusion of protoplasm), KARYOGAMY (fusion of the two nuclei) and MEIOSIS - producing sexual spores.

CLASSIFICATION OF FUNGI. Fungi are classified mainly by the structure of their mycelium and the way they produce sexual spores into four classes. (1) PHYCOMYCETES (the 'lower fungi') have coenocytic (aseptate) hyphae and mostly live in water or on decaying matter; examples are Rhizopus (bread mould), Mucor and the downy mildews; asexual spores form in sporangia. (2) ASCOMYCETES (the 'sac fungi') have septate hyphae and produce sexual spores called ASCOSPORES inside a sac-like ASCUS; examples are yeast (Saccharomyces), Penicillium, Aspergillus and the edible morels. (3) BASIDIOMYCETES (the 'club fungi') have septate hyphae and bear sexual spores called BASIDIOSPORES on a club-shaped BASIDIUM; examples are mushrooms (Agaricus), bracket fungi, puffballs and the parasitic rusts and smuts. (4) DEUTEROMYCETES (the 'imperfect fungi', Fungi Imperfecti) is an artificial group for fungi in which only the asexual stage is known - no sexual stage has been observed; examples are Alternaria and Colletotrichum, and many cause plant and skin diseases. When their sexual stage is discovered they are moved to one of the other classes.

2.6 ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE, LICHENS AND MYCORRHIZA

ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE OF FUNGI. Fungi affect human life deeply. USEFUL fungi include YEAST (Saccharomyces), which ferments sugar to alcohol and carbon dioxide and is used in baking bread and brewing; PENICILLIUM, the blue-green mould from which the first antibiotic, penicillin, was obtained by Alexander Fleming, and which is used to flavour cheeses; edible MUSHROOMS (Agaricus) grown as protein-rich food; and many fungi used to make organic acids, enzymes and vitamins, and as decomposers that recycle nutrients. HARMFUL fungi spoil food and cause many DISEASES: plant diseases such as wheat rust (Puccinia), potato late blight and smuts destroy crops; human diseases include ringworm, athlete's foot and other skin infections; and certain moulds produce poisonous toxins (such as aflatoxin) in stored grain.

LICHENS. A LICHEN is a close SYMBIOTIC partnership between a fungus (the mycobiont, usually an ascomycete) and a photosynthetic partner (the phycobiont - an alga or a cyanobacterium). The fungus provides shelter, water and minerals and anchors the lichen, while the alga or cyanobacterium makes food by photosynthesis (and, if a cyanobacterium, may also fix nitrogen). Together they can grow where neither could survive alone - on bare rock, tree bark and in the Arctic. Lichens are PIONEER colonisers that begin soil formation, and because they are very sensitive to air pollution (especially sulphur dioxide) they serve as natural INDICATORS OF AIR QUALITY.

MYCORRHIZA. A MYCORRHIZA ('fungus-root') is a symbiotic association between a fungus and the roots of a higher plant. The fungal hyphae greatly increase the surface area of the root and absorb water and mineral nutrients (especially phosphorus) from the soil, passing them to the plant; in return the plant supplies the fungus with sugars made in photosynthesis. Mycorrhizae help many trees and crop plants grow better, and some plants cannot establish themselves without their fungal partner.

2.7 A NOTE ON VIRUSES

VIRUSES are placed OUTSIDE the five kingdoms because they are ACELLULAR - they are not made of cells. A virus is an extremely small particle consisting of a core of nucleic acid (either DNA or RNA, never both) enclosed in a protein coat called a CAPSID. Viruses are obligate parasites: outside a living host cell they are inert and show no signs of life, but once inside a suitable host cell they take over its machinery to make thousands of new virus particles. Because they show characteristics of both living and non-living things, viruses are often called a bridge between the living and the non-living. They cause many diseases - such as polio, influenza, AIDS, COVID-19 and the common cold in humans, and mosaic diseases in plants. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria.

SUMMARY

- Kingdom Monera contains all prokaryotes - cells with no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; their DNA lies naked in a nucleoid.
- Bacteria occur as cocci, bacilli, spirilla and vibrios; they have a peptidoglycan cell wall, and are divided by Gram staining into Gram-positive (thick wall, purple) and Gram-negative (thin wall, pink).
- Bacterial nutrition is autotrophic (photo- or chemo-) or heterotrophic (saprophytic, parasitic, symbiotic); they reproduce by binary fission and exchange genes by conjugation, transformation and transduction.
- Bacteria decompose matter, fix nitrogen, make curd, vinegar and antibiotics, but also cause diseases such as cholera, tuberculosis and typhoid.
- Archaebacteria (methanogens, halophiles, thermoacidophiles) lack peptidoglycan and live in extreme habitats; eubacteria are the true, peptidoglycan-walled bacteria.
- Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes; many fix nitrogen using heterocysts and act as natural fertilisers. Mycoplasmas are the smallest cells and have no cell wall.
- Kingdom Protoctista contains simple eukaryotes: protozoa (Amoeba with pseudopodia, Paramecium with cilia, Plasmodium causing malaria), photosynthetic protists (Chlamydomonas, diatoms, dinoflagellates, euglenoids) and slime moulds.
- Kingdom Fungi are non-green heterotrophic eukaryotes with a body of hyphae forming a mycelium and a chitin cell wall; nutrition is saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic, with extracellular digestion.
- Fungi are classified into Phycomycetes (Rhizopus), Ascomycetes (yeast, Penicillium), Basidiomycetes (mushrooms, rusts) and Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi).
- Yeast is used in baking and brewing, Penicillium gives penicillin, mushrooms are eaten; fungi also cause rusts, smuts, ringworm and food spoilage.
- A lichen is a fungus-alga/cyanobacterium symbiosis and a pioneer and pollution indicator; a mycorrhiza is a fungus-root symbiosis that helps plants absorb minerals.
- Viruses are acellular obligate parasites (nucleic acid plus a protein capsid), a bridge between the living and non-living, and lie outside the five kingdoms.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - The Kingdoms Monera, Protoctista and Fungi (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer briefly and precisely; give examples where asked. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: Name the four basic shapes of bacteria and give one example of each.
questions.answer: The four basic shapes of bacteria are: (1) Coccus - spherical, e.g. Streptococcus; (2) Bacillus - rod-shaped, e.g. Lactobacillus; (3) Spirillum - rigid spiral, e.g. Spirillum; and (4) Vibrio - comma-shaped, e.g. Vibrio cholerae.
questions.explanation: Bacteria are grouped by shape into cocci, bacilli, spirilla and vibrios.

questions.question: Distinguish between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
questions.answer: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan cell wall and retain the violet stain, appearing purple. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer covered by an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane; they lose the violet stain and take up the red counterstain, appearing pink. The difference reflects wall structure and affects antibiotic sensitivity.
questions.explanation: The Gram reaction depends on the thickness of the peptidoglycan wall.

questions.question: What is conjugation in bacteria? How does it differ from binary fission?
questions.answer: Conjugation is a means of genetic recombination in which two bacteria join through a tube (formed with the help of a sex pilus) and a copy of DNA, often a plasmid, passes from a donor to a recipient cell. It creates genetic variation but does not increase cell number. Binary fission, by contrast, is asexual reproduction in which one cell copies its DNA and divides into two identical daughter cells, increasing the number of bacteria without genetic mixing.
questions.explanation: Conjugation transfers genes; binary fission multiplies cells.

questions.question: State two useful and two harmful roles of bacteria.
questions.answer: Useful roles: (1) decomposition of dead matter and recycling of nutrients in the soil; (2) nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium, and making curd (Lactobacillus), vinegar and antibiotics. Harmful roles: (1) spoilage of food; (2) causing diseases such as cholera, tuberculosis and typhoid.
questions.explanation: Bacteria are both beneficial (decay, nitrogen fixation, food, antibiotics) and harmful (spoilage, disease).

questions.question: How do archaebacteria differ from eubacteria? Name the three main types of archaebacteria.
questions.answer: Archaebacteria are ancient prokaryotes that lack peptidoglycan in their cell walls and have a distinctive membrane chemistry, which lets them survive extreme habitats; eubacteria are the true bacteria with peptidoglycan walls living in ordinary habitats. The three main types of archaebacteria are methanogens (produce methane), halophiles (live in very salty water) and thermoacidophiles (live in hot, acidic springs).
questions.explanation: Archaebacteria lack peptidoglycan and are extremophiles; methanogens, halophiles, thermoacidophiles.

questions.question: Describe the role of cyanobacteria in nitrogen fixation and explain why they are called natural fertilisers. Also explain what mycoplasmas are.
questions.answer: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are photosynthetic prokaryotes containing chlorophyll a and phycocyanin. Filamentous forms such as Nostoc and Anabaena possess special thick-walled cells called heterocysts in which they FIX atmospheric nitrogen (N2) into a usable combined form. Because they add both organic matter (through photosynthesis) and fixed nitrogen to the soil and water, they enrich paddy fields naturally and are therefore called natural or biological fertilisers, reducing the need for chemical nitrogen fertilisers. Mycoplasmas are the smallest known free-living cells and the simplest organisms; they are unique among prokaryotes in having NO cell wall, so they are variable in shape (pleomorphic) and are not affected by antibiotics such as penicillin that act on the wall. Some cause diseases in plants and animals, for example pleuropneumonia in cattle.
questions.explanation: Heterocysts fix nitrogen; cyanobacteria enrich soil; mycoplasmas are wall-less smallest cells.

questions.question: How do Amoeba and Paramecium move? Name the parasite that causes malaria and its insect carrier.
questions.answer: Amoeba moves and feeds using pseudopodia - temporary finger-like extensions of its cytoplasm. Paramecium moves by the beating of thousands of tiny hair-like cilia covering its body. Malaria is caused by the sporozoan parasite Plasmodium, which is carried by the female Anopheles mosquito.
questions.explanation: Amoeba - pseudopodia; Paramecium - cilia; Plasmodium via female Anopheles causes malaria.

questions.question: Why is Euglena considered a link between plants and animals?
questions.answer: Euglena has a green chloroplast and can photosynthesise like a plant when light is available. However, in the dark it loses its chlorophyll and feeds on organic matter like an animal. It also moves actively using a flagellum and has an eyespot, and lacks a rigid cellulose wall (it has a flexible pellicle). Because it shows features of both plants (photosynthesis) and animals (heterotrophic nutrition and active movement), Euglena is regarded as a link or bridge between plants and animals.
questions.explanation: Euglena photosynthesises in light but feeds like an animal in the dark.

questions.question: Describe the structure and nutrition of fungi. Name the four classes of fungi with one example of each.
questions.answer: Structure: except for the single-celled yeasts, a fungus body is made of fine thread-like filaments called hyphae; a mass of hyphae forms a mycelium that spreads through the food and absorbs nutrients. Hyphae may be septate (divided by cross-walls) or coenocytic (continuous, multinucleate). The cell wall is made of chitin, not cellulose, and reserve food is stored as glycogen. Nutrition: all fungi are heterotrophic and carry out extracellular digestion - they secrete enzymes onto the food, which is broken down outside the body and then absorbed. The three modes are saprophytic (on dead matter, e.g. Rhizopus), parasitic (on a living host, causing disease) and symbiotic (as in lichens and mycorrhizae). Four classes: (1) Phycomycetes - Rhizopus (bread mould); (2) Ascomycetes - Penicillium/yeast; (3) Basidiomycetes - Agaricus (mushroom); (4) Deuteromycetes - Alternaria.
questions.explanation: Hyphae/mycelium, chitin wall, extracellular heterotrophic nutrition; four classes with examples.

questions.question: What is a lichen? Explain the symbiotic relationship in a lichen and state why lichens are used as indicators of air pollution. Also define mycorrhiza.
questions.answer: A lichen is a close symbiotic association between a fungus (the mycobiont, usually an ascomycete) and a photosynthetic partner (the phycobiont - an alga or a cyanobacterium). The fungus provides shelter, anchorage, water and minerals and protects the partner, while the alga or cyanobacterium makes food by photosynthesis (and, if a cyanobacterium, may also fix nitrogen); both partners benefit, so the two can grow on bare rock and bark where neither could live alone. Lichens are very sensitive to air pollutants, especially sulphur dioxide, and die where the air is dirty, so their presence or absence indicates air quality; hence they are natural indicators of air pollution. A mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association between a fungus and the roots of a higher plant, in which the fungus helps the plant absorb water and minerals (especially phosphorus) and receives sugars in return.
questions.explanation: Lichen = fungus + alga/cyanobacterium symbiosis; pollution indicator; mycorrhiza = fungus-root symbiosis.

questions.question: Define a prokaryote and give two examples.
questions.answer: A prokaryote is an organism whose cell has no true membrane-bound nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; its DNA lies naked in a nucleoid. Examples: bacteria and cyanobacteria.
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes lack a true nucleus; e.g. bacteria, cyanobacteria.

questions.question: List any three structures found in a bacterial cell and give the function of each.
questions.answer: (1) Cell wall (peptidoglycan) - gives shape and protection; (2) Plasma membrane - controls entry/exit of substances and carries out respiration; (3) Nucleoid - contains the circular DNA that controls the cell. (Flagella provide movement; plasmids carry extra genes.)
questions.explanation: Any three: wall, membrane, nucleoid, flagella, plasmid, ribosomes with functions.

questions.question: What is an endospore and what is its significance?
questions.answer: An endospore is a thick-walled, dormant resting structure formed inside certain bacteria (such as Bacillus and Clostridium) under unfavourable conditions. It is highly resistant to heat, drought and chemicals and can survive for years, germinating into an active bacterium when conditions become favourable again. It helps the bacterium survive harsh environments.
questions.explanation: Endospore = resistant resting stage for survival.

questions.question: Name the three ways in which bacteria exchange genetic material and describe one.
questions.answer: The three ways are conjugation, transformation and transduction. In conjugation, two bacteria join through a tube formed with a sex pilus and a copy of DNA (often a plasmid) passes from a donor to a recipient cell, creating genetic variation.
questions.explanation: Conjugation, transformation, transduction; describe conjugation.

questions.question: Explain how bacteria are useful in agriculture.
questions.answer: Bacteria are useful in agriculture mainly through nitrogen fixation and decomposition. Symbiotic Rhizobium in legume root nodules and free-living Azotobacter fix atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use, enriching soil fertility. Saprophytic bacteria decompose dead plant and animal matter, recycling nutrients back into the soil. Together they maintain soil fertility and reduce the need for chemical fertilisers.
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium) and decomposition enrich soil.

questions.question: Name any two diseases caused by bacteria and the bacterium responsible for each.
questions.answer: (1) Cholera - caused by Vibrio cholerae; (2) Tuberculosis - caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. (Others: typhoid - Salmonella typhi; tetanus - Clostridium tetani.)
questions.explanation: Two bacterial diseases with causative organisms.

questions.question: Give two differences between archaebacteria and eubacteria.
questions.answer: (1) Archaebacteria lack peptidoglycan in their cell walls, whereas eubacteria have peptidoglycan walls. (2) Archaebacteria live in extreme habitats (very salty, hot-acidic, marshy places) and have a distinctive membrane chemistry, while eubacteria are the ordinary true bacteria of common habitats.
questions.explanation: Wall chemistry (no peptidoglycan) and extreme habitats distinguish archaebacteria.

questions.question: Why are cyanobacteria important in paddy (rice) fields?
questions.answer: In paddy fields, filamentous cyanobacteria such as Anabaena and Nostoc fix atmospheric nitrogen in their heterocysts and add it, along with organic matter from photosynthesis, to the waterlogged soil. This natural enrichment increases soil fertility and rice yield, so cyanobacteria act as natural biofertilisers and reduce the need for chemical nitrogen fertilisers.
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria fix nitrogen and enrich paddy soil as biofertilisers.

questions.question: State two special features of mycoplasmas.
questions.answer: (1) Mycoplasmas are the smallest known free-living cells and the simplest organisms. (2) They have no cell wall, so they are variable in shape and are not affected by antibiotics such as penicillin that act on the wall.
questions.explanation: Smallest cells; lack a cell wall.

questions.question: Name the kingdom to which Amoeba, Paramecium and Plasmodium belong and state one common feature.
questions.answer: They all belong to Kingdom Protoctista (Protista). A common feature is that they are simple, single-celled eukaryotes (protozoa) with a true membrane-bound nucleus.
questions.explanation: All are protozoan protists - unicellular eukaryotes.

questions.question: Describe how Paramecium feeds.
questions.answer: Paramecium is covered with thousands of tiny beating hairs called cilia. The cilia sweep water and food particles towards a groove on the side of the body called the oral groove, which leads food into the cell where it is enclosed in food vacuoles and digested. Undigested matter is expelled from the cell.
questions.explanation: Cilia sweep food into the oral groove; digested in food vacuoles.

questions.question: How is malaria transmitted, and how can knowing the vector help control the disease?
questions.answer: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium, which is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. Because the mosquito is the vector, controlling malaria depends on destroying mosquitoes and their breeding places - draining stagnant water, spraying insecticides and using mosquito nets - so as to break the chain of transmission.
questions.explanation: Plasmodium via female Anopheles; control the vector to control malaria.

questions.question: Mention two uses or importance of diatoms.
questions.answer: (1) Diatoms are a major part of the phytoplankton, forming the base of aquatic food chains and producing much of the world's oxygen. (2) Their indestructible silica walls accumulate as diatomaceous earth, which is used as a polishing agent, filter and abrasive.
questions.explanation: Diatoms are food-chain base and yield diatomaceous earth.

questions.question: What is a red tide and how is it harmful?
questions.answer: A red tide is the rapid multiplication (bloom) of certain dinoflagellates that colours seawater red or brown. These blooms release toxins into the water that can kill fish and other marine animals, and may poison people who eat contaminated shellfish, so red tides are harmful to marine life and human health.
questions.explanation: Red tide = toxic dinoflagellate bloom that kills marine life.

questions.question: How does a slime mould reproduce when conditions become unfavourable?
questions.answer: When the surroundings become dry or food is scarce, the creeping multinucleate plasmodium of a slime mould stops moving and differentiates into many stalked fruiting bodies. These fruiting bodies produce resistant spores with true walls; the spores are dispersed and remain dormant, germinating into new individuals when favourable conditions return.
questions.explanation: Plasmodium forms fruiting bodies that release resistant spores.

questions.question: Differentiate between septate and coenocytic hyphae.
questions.answer: Septate hyphae are divided into cells by cross-walls called septa, so each compartment usually has one or a few nuclei. Coenocytic (aseptate) hyphae have no cross-walls; they are continuous tubes of multinucleate cytoplasm, as in Phycomycetes such as Rhizopus.
questions.explanation: Septate = cross-walls present; coenocytic = no cross-walls, multinucleate.

questions.question: Describe the three modes of nutrition found in fungi with one example each.
questions.answer: (1) Saprophytic - feeding on dead organic matter, e.g. Rhizopus (bread mould). (2) Parasitic - living on or in a living host and causing disease, e.g. Puccinia (wheat rust). (3) Symbiotic - living in a mutually beneficial partnership, e.g. the fungus in a lichen or mycorrhiza.
questions.explanation: Saprophytic, parasitic and symbiotic modes with examples.

questions.question: What is meant by extracellular digestion in fungi?
questions.answer: Extracellular digestion means that fungi digest their food outside their bodies. They secrete digestive enzymes onto the food (dead matter or a host's tissues); the enzymes break the food down into simple soluble substances, which the fungal hyphae then absorb. Digestion therefore happens outside the cell before absorption.
questions.explanation: Enzymes secreted onto food; digested outside, then absorbed.

questions.question: On what basis are fungi classified into their four classes? Name the classes.
questions.answer: Fungi are classified mainly on the basis of the structure of their hyphae (septate or coenocytic) and the type of sexual spores they produce. The four classes are Phycomycetes, Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes and Deuteromycetes.
questions.explanation: Basis = hyphal structure + sexual spore type; four classes named.

questions.question: A fungus has septate hyphae and bears its spores on club-shaped basidia. To which class does it belong and give an example.
questions.answer: A fungus with septate hyphae bearing spores (basidiospores) on club-shaped basidia belongs to the class Basidiomycetes. An example is the common mushroom, Agaricus. (Rusts and smuts are also basidiomycetes.)
questions.explanation: Septate hyphae + basidia = Basidiomycetes, e.g. Agaricus.

questions.question: Explain why lichens can grow on bare rock where no other plant survives.
questions.answer: In a lichen, a fungus and an alga (or cyanobacterium) live in symbiosis. The fungus anchors the lichen to the rock and absorbs and stores water and minerals, protecting the alga from drying out, while the alga or cyanobacterium makes food by photosynthesis (and may fix nitrogen). Because each partner supplies what the other lacks, together they can survive on bare rock where neither could live alone, and they act as pioneer colonisers that begin soil formation.
questions.explanation: Fungal water/mineral supply plus algal food let lichens pioneer bare rock.

questions.question: What is a virus? Why is it called a bridge between the living and the non-living?
questions.answer: A virus is an extremely small, acellular particle made of a core of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat called a capsid. Outside a host it is inert like a non-living chemical, but inside a living host cell it reproduces and behaves like a living thing. Because it shows properties of both the non-living (inert, crystallisable outside) and the living (reproduction inside a host), it is called a bridge between the living and the non-living.
questions.explanation: Virus = nucleic acid + capsid; inert outside, active inside host.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a typical bacterial cell, naming its main parts and their functions.
questions.answer: A bacterial cell is a prokaryotic cell. On the outside is a rigid cell wall made of peptidoglycan, which gives shape and protection; many bacteria also have a gelatinous capsule outside the wall that helps them stick to surfaces and resist host defences. Beneath the wall is the plasma membrane, which controls the entry and exit of substances and carries out respiration (there being no mitochondria). The cytoplasm contains 70S ribosomes for protein synthesis, food reserves, and the nucleoid - a region holding the single circular DNA molecule that controls the cell. Many bacteria carry small extra circular DNA molecules called plasmids, which often bear antibiotic-resistance genes. Some cells bear whip-like flagella for movement and fine hair-like pili for attachment and conjugation. Under harsh conditions certain bacteria form a thick-walled resting endospore that survives heat and drought.
questions.explanation: Wall, capsule, membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, nucleoid, plasmid, flagella, pili, endospore with functions.

questions.question: Discuss the economic importance of bacteria, giving both useful and harmful roles.
questions.answer: Bacteria are of great economic importance, both beneficial and harmful. Useful roles: (1) Decomposition - saprophytic bacteria decay dead plants and animals, recycling nutrients and keeping the environment clean. (2) Nitrogen fixation - Rhizobium in legume nodules and free-living Azotobacter enrich the soil with nitrogen. (3) Dairy and food - Lactobacillus turns milk into curd and cheese; bacteria also make vinegar. (4) Medicine and industry - antibiotics such as streptomycin (from Streptomyces), vitamins, enzymes and, through genetic engineering, insulin are produced using bacteria. (5) Retting of fibres like jute. Harmful roles: (1) Food spoilage. (2) Human diseases such as cholera (Vibrio cholerae), tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), typhoid (Salmonella typhi) and tetanus (Clostridium tetani). (3) Plant diseases such as citrus canker and animal diseases such as anthrax. Thus bacteria are indispensable in nature and industry but also cause serious diseases and losses.
questions.explanation: Balanced account: decay, N-fixation, dairy, antibiotics vs spoilage and disease.

questions.question: Describe cyanobacteria under the headings: structure, pigments, nitrogen fixation and importance.
questions.answer: Structure: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are photosynthetic prokaryotes that may be single-celled, colonial or filamentous (e.g. Nostoc, Anabaena, Oscillatoria, Spirulina), often surrounded by a gelatinous sheath; they have no true nucleus or membrane-bound chloroplast. Pigments: they contain chlorophyll a and the blue pigment phycocyanin (and sometimes red phycoerythrin), which give them their characteristic blue-green colour, and they carry out oxygen-releasing photosynthesis. Nitrogen fixation: many filamentous forms have special thick-walled cells called heterocysts in which atmospheric nitrogen is fixed into a usable combined form. Importance: they were probably the first organisms to oxygenate the early atmosphere; they act as natural biofertilisers in paddy fields; Spirulina is grown as a protein-rich food; but in nutrient-rich water they can form water blooms that pollute water bodies.
questions.explanation: Structure, pigments (chl a, phycocyanin), heterocyst N-fixation, importance/blooms.

questions.question: Compare Amoeba, Paramecium and Plasmodium with respect to locomotion, nutrition and importance.
questions.answer: Amoeba: moves and feeds using pseudopodia (temporary cytoplasmic projections); nutrition is holozoic - it engulfs food particles by phagocytosis; it is free-living in water and important in food chains; reproduces by binary fission. Paramecium: a slipper-shaped ciliate that moves by beating thousands of cilia; it sweeps food into an oral groove and digests it in food vacuoles; it is free-living, has two nuclei and can undergo conjugation; important in aquatic food chains. Plasmodium: a sporozoan that has no organs of locomotion; it is a parasite that lives inside human red blood cells and the female Anopheles mosquito; nutrition is parasitic, absorbing nourishment from the host; it is medically important as the cause of malaria. Thus the three differ in locomotory organ (pseudopodia, cilia, none), nutrition (holozoic, holozoic, parasitic) and importance (ecological vs disease).
questions.explanation: Systematic comparison of the three protozoa on locomotion, nutrition, importance.

questions.question: Write an account of the main groups of photosynthetic protists.
questions.answer: Photosynthetic (plant-like) protists carry chlorophyll and make their own food, forming much of the phytoplankton. (1) Chlamydomonas is a single-celled green alga with two flagella, a cup-shaped chloroplast and a light-sensitive eyespot. (2) Diatoms are golden-brown algae enclosed in two-piece silica walls that fit together like a box; their walls accumulate as diatomaceous earth, used as a filter and polish, and they are major oxygen producers. (3) Dinoflagellates are mostly marine, spinning with two flagella; some are luminescent, and certain species form toxic red tides. (4) Euglenoids such as Euglena have a chloroplast and photosynthesise in light but feed like animals in the dark; they have a flexible pellicle, a flagellum and an eyespot, and are considered a link between plants and animals. Together these protists form the base of aquatic food chains and produce a large share of the Earth's oxygen.
questions.explanation: Chlamydomonas, diatoms, dinoflagellates, euglenoids described with features and roles.

questions.question: Describe the four classes of fungi, giving the distinguishing features and examples of each.
questions.answer: Fungi are classified by hyphal structure and sexual spores into four classes. (1) Phycomycetes ('lower fungi') - coenocytic (aseptate) hyphae; live in water or on decaying matter; asexual spores form in sporangia; e.g. Rhizopus (bread mould), Mucor. (2) Ascomycetes ('sac fungi') - septate hyphae; sexual spores called ascospores form inside a sac-like ascus; e.g. yeast (Saccharomyces), Penicillium, Aspergillus, morels. (3) Basidiomycetes ('club fungi') - septate hyphae; sexual spores called basidiospores are borne on a club-shaped basidium; e.g. mushrooms (Agaricus), bracket fungi, puffballs, rusts and smuts. (4) Deuteromycetes ('imperfect fungi') - an artificial group of fungi in which only the asexual stage is known and no sexual stage has been observed; e.g. Alternaria, Colletotrichum; many cause plant and skin diseases, and are reclassified once their sexual stage is found.
questions.explanation: Four classes with hyphal type, sexual spore, and examples.

questions.question: 'The class Deuteromycetes is not a natural group.' Analyse this statement and explain how such fungi are treated once more is known about them.
questions.answer: Deuteromycetes, also called the Fungi Imperfecti or 'imperfect fungi', is an artificial or form group rather than a natural class. Members are placed in it only because their sexual (perfect) stage has not been observed - they are known solely by their asexual reproduction (usually conidia) and by septate hyphae. Because classification of the other three classes is based on the type of sexual spore produced, a fungus whose sexual stage is unknown cannot be placed naturally, so it is kept temporarily in Deuteromycetes. This is why the group does not reflect true evolutionary relationships; it simply collects fungi awaiting proper placement. When the sexual stage of such a fungus is later discovered - for example, an ascus or a basidium - the fungus is removed from Deuteromycetes and transferred to Ascomycetes or Basidiomycetes as appropriate. Thus Deuteromycetes is a 'holding' group based on incomplete knowledge, which is why it is regarded as an unnatural, artificial class. Many important disease-causing fungi (e.g. Alternaria) are placed here.
questions.explanation: Deuteromycetes = artificial group based on missing sexual stage; reclassified when found.

questions.question: Evaluate the roles of fungi in human welfare, giving both beneficial and harmful examples.
questions.answer: Fungi have a deep and mixed impact on human welfare. Beneficial roles: (1) Food and fermentation - yeast (Saccharomyces) ferments sugar to alcohol and carbon dioxide and is used in baking bread and brewing; edible mushrooms (Agaricus) are grown as protein-rich food; Penicillium flavours cheeses. (2) Medicine - Penicillium yields the antibiotic penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming; other fungi give further antibiotics and organic acids, enzymes and vitamins. (3) Ecology - saprophytic fungi decompose dead matter and recycle nutrients, and mycorrhizal fungi help plants absorb minerals. Harmful roles: (1) Plant diseases such as wheat rust (Puccinia), potato late blight and smuts destroy crops and cause huge losses. (2) Human diseases such as ringworm and athlete's foot are caused by fungi. (3) Spoilage of food and the production of poisonous toxins such as aflatoxin in stored grain. On balance, fungi are essential decomposers and sources of food and medicine, yet they also cause serious diseases and economic losses, so their role in human welfare is both indispensable and, at times, damaging.
questions.explanation: Balanced evaluation: food, medicine, ecology vs crop/human disease and spoilage.

questions.question: A microbiologist stains a mixed sample of bacteria by Gram's method and examines it. Some cells appear purple and spherical in clusters, while others appear pink and rod-shaped. (a) Which cells are Gram-positive and which are Gram-negative? (b) What structural difference explains the two colours? (c) Name the shape category of each type.
questions.answer: (a) The purple cells are Gram-positive and the pink cells are Gram-negative. (b) Gram-positive cells have a thick peptidoglycan wall that retains the violet stain, giving a purple colour; Gram-negative cells have a thin peptidoglycan layer with an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane, so they lose the violet stain and take up the red counterstain, appearing pink. (c) The purple spherical cells in clusters are cocci (staphylococci); the pink rod-shaped cells are bacilli.
questions.explanation: Purple=Gram+ (thick wall, cocci); pink=Gram- (thin wall, bacilli).

questions.question: In a hospital, a strain of bacteria that was once killed by an antibiotic is now found to survive it. Investigation shows the resistant cells carry a plasmid that is passed to other cells. (a) Name the plasmid-based process that spreads the resistance. (b) How does binary fission then increase the number of resistant cells? (c) Suggest one way to slow the spread of resistance.
questions.answer: (a) The resistance gene is spread by conjugation, in which a copy of the resistance plasmid passes from a donor to a recipient cell through a tube. (b) Once a cell is resistant, binary fission rapidly copies its DNA and divides it into two identical resistant daughter cells, so the resistant population multiplies quickly. (c) The spread can be slowed by using antibiotics carefully and only when necessary, completing prescribed courses, and maintaining good hygiene to reduce infection - so that fewer resistant strains are selected and passed on.
questions.explanation: Conjugation spreads plasmid; binary fission multiplies resistant cells; prudent antibiotic use slows it.

questions.question: A farmer notices that a pond and paddy field covered with a blue-green scum of Anabaena and Nostoc gives better rice growth without added nitrogen fertiliser. (a) To which kingdom do these organisms belong? (b) How do they add nitrogen to the field? (c) Name the special cell involved.
questions.answer: (a) Anabaena and Nostoc are cyanobacteria and belong to Kingdom Monera (they are prokaryotes). (b) They fix atmospheric nitrogen (N2) into a usable combined form and, together with organic matter from photosynthesis, add it to the waterlogged soil, so they act as natural biofertilisers that improve rice growth without chemical nitrogen. (c) Nitrogen fixation takes place in special thick-walled cells called heterocysts.
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria (Monera) fix nitrogen in heterocysts and act as biofertilisers.

questions.question: A patient with recurring fever is diagnosed with malaria after a blood test shows a parasite inside the red blood cells. The doctor advises removing stagnant water around the house. (a) Name the parasite and the kingdom it belongs to. (b) How is it transmitted? (c) Why does removing stagnant water help?
questions.answer: (a) The parasite is Plasmodium, which belongs to Kingdom Protoctista (it is a protozoan, a sporozoan). (b) It is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. (c) Female Anopheles mosquitoes breed in stagnant water; removing stagnant water destroys their breeding places, reduces the mosquito population, and so breaks the chain of transmission and helps control malaria.
questions.explanation: Plasmodium (protist) via female Anopheles; remove stagnant water to stop mosquito breeding.

questions.question: A student keeps Euglena in a jar. In sunlight the water turns green and the organisms make food; when the jar is kept in the dark for several days, the green colour fades but the organisms are still alive and feeding. (a) Explain the change in nutrition. (b) Why is Euglena called a link between plants and animals? (c) Name the structure Euglena uses to move.
questions.answer: (a) In sunlight Euglena uses its chloroplast to photosynthesise and make its own food (autotrophic, plant-like nutrition), which turns the water green. In the dark it cannot photosynthesise, loses its chlorophyll and instead feeds on organic matter from the surroundings (heterotrophic, animal-like nutrition), so it survives even though the green colour fades. (b) Because it shows plant features (chloroplast, photosynthesis) and animal features (heterotrophic feeding and active movement), Euglena is called a link or bridge between plants and animals. (c) Euglena moves using a whip-like flagellum.
questions.explanation: Euglena switches from photosynthesis to animal-like feeding; hence plant-animal link; moves by flagellum.

questions.question: A slice of moist bread left in the open for a few days develops a cottony white growth that later shows tiny black rounded structures. Under the microscope, aseptate thread-like filaments are seen. (a) Name the fungus and its class. (b) What are the thread-like filaments and the black structures? (c) State the mode of nutrition.
questions.answer: (a) The fungus is Rhizopus (the common bread mould), which belongs to the class Phycomycetes. (b) The cottony threads are hyphae (which together form the mycelium); the hyphae here are coenocytic (aseptate), and the tiny black rounded structures are sporangia that contain asexual spores. (c) Its mode of nutrition is saprophytic - it secretes enzymes onto the bread, digests the food externally and absorbs the products (extracellular digestion).
questions.explanation: Rhizopus (Phycomycetes); coenocytic hyphae + sporangia; saprophytic extracellular nutrition.

questions.question: Three unknown fungi are examined. Fungus A has coenocytic hyphae and forms spores in sporangia. Fungus B has septate hyphae and forms spores inside a sac. Fungus C has septate hyphae and bears spores on a club-shaped structure. (a) Classify A, B and C. (b) Name the sexual spore of B and C. (c) Give one example of each class.
questions.answer: (a) Fungus A (coenocytic hyphae, sporangia) is a Phycomycete; Fungus B (septate hyphae, spores in a sac/ascus) is an Ascomycete; Fungus C (septate hyphae, spores on a club-shaped basidium) is a Basidiomycete. (b) The sexual spore of B (Ascomycetes) is the ascospore; the sexual spore of C (Basidiomycetes) is the basidiospore. (c) Examples: A - Rhizopus; B - Penicillium (or yeast); C - Agaricus (mushroom).
questions.explanation: Classify by hyphae + spore structure; ascospore vs basidiospore; examples.

questions.question: A city environmental survey finds that lichens grow abundantly on tree bark in the outskirts but are absent in the polluted city centre. (a) What is a lichen made of? (b) Why are lichens absent from the polluted centre? (c) How can lichens be used practically from this observation?
questions.answer: (a) A lichen is a symbiotic association of a fungus (usually an ascomycete) with an alga or a cyanobacterium; the fungus provides shelter, water and minerals and the alga/cyanobacterium makes food by photosynthesis. (b) Lichens are very sensitive to air pollutants, especially sulphur dioxide; in the heavily polluted city centre the dirty air kills them, so they are absent there. (c) Because their presence or absence reflects air quality, lichens can be used practically as natural indicators (bioindicators) of air pollution - abundant lichens mean clean air, while their absence signals polluted air.
questions.explanation: Lichen = fungus+alga/cyanobacterium; killed by SO2; used as air-pollution bioindicators.

questions.question: A forester finds that pine seedlings planted in sterilised soil grow poorly, but seedlings whose roots are wrapped in a fungal sheath grow vigorously and absorb minerals well. (a) Name the association between the fungus and the root. (b) How does each partner benefit? (c) Why did seedlings in sterilised soil grow poorly?
questions.answer: (a) The association between the fungus and the plant root is called a mycorrhiza. (b) The fungus benefits by receiving sugars made by the plant in photosynthesis; the plant benefits because the fungal hyphae greatly increase the root surface and absorb water and minerals (especially phosphorus) from the soil, improving the plant's growth. (c) The sterilised soil lacked the fungal partner, so the seedlings had no mycorrhiza to help them absorb minerals efficiently and therefore grew poorly - showing that some plants depend on their fungal partner to establish well.
questions.explanation: Mycorrhiza = fungus-root symbiosis; fungus gets sugars, plant gets minerals; no fungus = poor growth.

questions.question: Bacteria are found almost everywhere - in soil, water, air, hot springs and inside other organisms - and can multiply every 20 minutes under good conditions. Some form endospores in bad conditions. (a) What feature of their cell makes bacteria prokaryotic? (b) How do they multiply so fast? (c) How do endospores help survival?
questions.answer: (a) Bacteria are prokaryotic because their cells have no true membrane-bound nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; their circular DNA lies naked in a region called the nucleoid. (b) They multiply fast by binary fission, in which a cell copies its DNA and simply divides into two identical daughter cells; under ideal conditions this can happen about every 20 minutes, so numbers grow explosively. (c) Under harsh conditions certain bacteria form thick-walled endospores that resist heat, drought and chemicals and can remain dormant for years, germinating into active cells when conditions again become favourable - so endospores ensure survival through bad times.
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic (nucleoid); rapid binary fission; endospores resist harsh conditions.
